summary: Soudein Circular Metals, Inc. (Buyer, the firm's client) bought all outstanding stock of Volterren Recovery Corp., a lithium-ion and lead-acid battery recycling company with a hydrometallurgical black-mass facility in Rochester, New York, from Brurir Industrial Partners LLC (Seller). The Purchase Price was $86,400,000, with $8,640,000 held in escrow. The Stock Purchase Agreement was signed July 28, 2025 and closed September 30, 2025. The folder also holds the closing documents and later documents: a Disclosure Schedule, an Escrow Agreement, a post-closing Side Letter dated November 20, 2025, the founder's IP Assignment Agreement and Key Employee Agreement, a Bill of Sale for Seller-owned shredding equipment, the May 2025 Letter of Intent, the Company's Buffalo office lease, and Buyer board resolutions. Six problems are planted. (1) The Escrow Agreement chooses Delaware law and a Delaware forum, and controls escrow matters. (2) General representations survive only until a 90-day escrow release date. (3) The founder's IP assignment reaches only inventions made during an employment period that begins after the core patent application was filed. (4) Buyer's working-capital dispute was raised after the 30-day dispute window had run. (5) The Side Letter amendment drops Environmental Matters from the Fundamental Representations. (6) The Bill of Sale gives an uncapped Buyer indemnity for pre-closing equipment liabilities.

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: Escrow Agreement Section 12 chooses Delaware law. It also gives the Delaware Court of Chancery exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute about entitlement to the Escrow Funds, 'notwithstanding any other agreement among the parties'. By contrast, SPA Sections 11.6 and 11.7 choose New York law and New York County courts for disputes under the SPA and any Ancillary Agreement. The SPA cannot cure the conflict. Its precedence clause (Section 11.9) expressly lets the Escrow Agreement govern the holding and release of the Escrow Funds. Read together, Buyer's indemnity claims would be decided on the merits in New York under New York law, while any fight over releasing the $8,640,000 escrow to pay them would go to Delaware under Delaware law. That risks parallel proceedings, inconsistent results and delay in reaching Buyer's main source of recovery.
issues.expected_finding: The Escrow Agreement's Delaware law and exclusive Delaware Chancery forum conflict with the SPA's New York law and New York County forum, and because SPA Section 11.9 lets the Escrow Agreement govern escrow release, Buyer faces split forums for its indemnity claims and escrow recovery; the parties and Escrow Agent should amend the Escrow Agreement to adopt New York law and forum.

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description: SPA Section 9.1 provides that representations other than Fundamental Representations survive until the 'General Survival Date'. SPA Section 1.1 defines that date as the Escrow Release Date as defined in the Escrow Agreement. Escrow Agreement Section 5.1 sets the Escrow Release Date at ninety days after the Closing Date. Measured from the September 30, 2025 Closing Date in SPA Section 3.1, the general representations therefore expire on December 29, 2025. That is far shorter than the 18-month survival agreed in Letter of Intent Section 4, and too short for Buyer to find breaches such as undisclosed permit or operational problems at a battery recycling plant. SPA Section 11.9 lets the Escrow Agreement govern release, so the 90-day date controls. Neither document alone shows the short survival period.
issues.expected_finding: Because the SPA ties general representation survival to an Escrow Release Date set at 90 days after the September 30, 2025 Closing, Buyer's claims for breach of general representations lapse on December 29, 2025 rather than the 18 months agreed in the Letter of Intent, and the survival period should be amended to run 18 months independent of the escrow release date.
detect_terms2: ninety (90) days after the Closing Date

issues.label: defined term inconsistency
issues.description: IP Assignment Agreement Section 1 assigns to the Company only 'Assigned Inventions'. These are defined as Inventions the founder conceived or developed 'during the Employment Period (as defined in the Key Employee Agreement)'. The recitals of the same agreement identify the Leaching Patent Application, filed September 14, 2021, as the founder's core hydrometallurgical lithium-recovery invention. Key Employee Agreement Section 1.1 defines the Employment Period as beginning on March 1, 2023. Read together, the Leaching Patent Application and all pre-2023 know-how fall outside the assignment, so the founder still owns them. This holds even though the SPA definition of Company Intellectual Property and Disclosure Schedule 3.10 treat them as Company-owned. Buyer's only recourse would be a representation claim, which is capped and short-lived.
issues.expected_finding: Because the IP Assignment Agreement covers only inventions made during an Employment Period that the Key Employee Agreement starts on March 1, 2023, the Leaching Patent Application filed September 14, 2021 was never assigned to the Company, and Buyer should obtain a confirmatory nunc pro tunc assignment from the founder covering all pre-employment inventions, including that application.

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description: SPA Section 2.4(c) gives Buyer thirty days after Seller delivers the Closing Statement to deliver a Dispute Notice. If Buyer does not, the Closing Statement becomes final and binding. Side Letter Section 3 records three things: Seller delivered the Closing Statement on October 17, 2025; Buyer disputes the Closing Net Working Capital, claiming a $1,275,000 shortfall; and each party reserves its rights. The Side Letter is dated November 20, 2025, and nothing in the folder shows an earlier Dispute Notice. The window closed on November 16, 2025, or November 17, 2025 if the deadline rolls to the next business day. Buyer's dispute is therefore late, and Seller can argue the Closing Statement is binding. The Side Letter shows Buyer has not accepted the Closing Statement and is still contesting it. The point is visible only by computing the SPA period from the delivery date recited in the Side Letter.
issues.expected_finding: Buyer's working-capital dispute, first raised in the November 20, 2025 Side Letter, came after the 30-day window that ran from Seller's October 17, 2025 delivery of the Closing Statement, so Seller can treat the Closing Statement as final and binding unless Buyer obtains Seller's written extension or waiver or shows an earlier timely Dispute Notice.
detect_terms2: disputes the Closing Net Working Capital

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description: SPA Section 1.1 defines Fundamental Representations to include Section 3.18 (Environmental Matters). Under SPA Sections 9.1 and 9.5(a), those representations survive six years and sit outside the 10% cap. Side Letter Section 2 is expressly an amendment under SPA Section 11.10, signed by Buyer and Seller. It redefines Fundamental Representations, 'for all purposes of Article IX', as Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 (Brokers). This silently drops Environmental Matters. Under SPA Section 11.9 a signed amendment citing Section 11.10 controls, so the change is effective. Pre-closing contamination is the main risk at a lead-acid and lithium-ion recycling site, and environmental claims are now capped at $8,640,000 and subject to the short General Survival Date.
issues.expected_finding: The Side Letter amendment removes the Environmental Matters representation (Section 3.18) from Fundamental Representations, and because it controls under SPA Section 11.9, environmental losses are now subject to the 10% cap and the short general survival period, so Buyer should seek a corrective amendment restoring Section 3.18 as a Fundamental Representation.

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: Bill of Sale Section 4 transfers Seller's Line 2 shredding and black-mass separation system to Buyer. Buyer assumes all Liabilities relating to the equipment 'whether arising before, at or after the Closing', including environmental claims from Seller's or the Company's pre-closing use, and indemnifies Seller for them. The clause states that Buyer's obligations 'shall not be subject to any limitation as to amount or time.' The SPA does not address liabilities for the transferred equipment, and its cap in Section 9.5(a) applies only to Seller's indemnity under Section 9.2(a). So there is no conflict for the precedence clause in SPA Section 11.9 to resolve. Buyer is left with unlimited, perpetual exposure for pre-closing contamination caused by Seller's equipment.
detect_terms: whether arising before, at or after the Closing
shall not be subject to any limitation as to amount or time
issues.expected_finding: The Bill of Sale makes Buyer assume and indemnify Seller, without any cap or time limit, for all liabilities of the transferred shredding equipment including pre-closing environmental liabilities, which the SPA does not limit, so Buyer should amend the Bill of Sale to exclude pre-closing liabilities and cap any Buyer indemnity.
